opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because research is full of choices that nobody tells you how to make. You're always deciding what to work on, what to drop, whom to work with, and when to keep going.

For me the first principle is to work on things I genuinely believe matter, not things that are fashionable or easy to publish. The field moves very fast, and it's tempting to chase whatever is hot this month. But if you only follow the crowd, you end up doing incremental work that someone else would have done two weeks later anyway. I'd rather ask: if this works, does it change how people think about the problem? If the answer is no, maybe it's not worth my time, even if it's a safe paper.

The second is honesty, both with yourself and with the community. It's very easy to fool yourself in research, especially in deep learning, where you can tune things until the numbers look good. I try to stay skeptical of my own results. Does this really hold up? Is it the idea, or is it some trick in the implementation? Some of the work I'm proudest of came from questioning assumptions everyone took for granted, and you can only do that if you're willing to question your own assumptions too.

Third, I think simplicity is underrated. I've always liked ideas that are simple and general, ones you can explain in a sentence. If a method needs ten complicated components to work, I'm usually suspicious it won't last. The ideas that survive over time tend to be clean.

And finally, taste and patience. Taste is something you build by reading broadly, looking at what has had lasting impact, and thinking about why. Patience means being willing to spend a long time on a problem you care about, even when it doesn't pay off right away. A lot of important things look unpromising at first.

So: work on what matters, be honest, keep it simple, and trust your taste while giving it time. Easy to say, hard to do, but that's what I try to follow.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should stay skeptical of their results, but does not say that a competitive research environment may erode that skepticism.

r002.rationale: It advises pursuing work that could change how people think about a problem instead of following fashionable topics or producing incremental work, expressing a principle of doing distinctive research.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because the field moves so fast that if you don't have some principles, you just get pulled in every direction.

The first one for me is: work on problems you genuinely find interesting, not the ones that are trendy right now. When I was doing ResNeXt, or later ConvNeXt, a lot of people thought ConvNets were basically done, everything was going to be Transformers. But I was curious whether that was really true or whether we just hadn't trained ConvNets properly. That curiosity turned out to matter more than following the trend. If you chase what's hot, by the time you publish, it's not hot anymore.

The second is simplicity. I have a strong bias toward simple ideas that actually work. If a method needs ten tricks to function, I don't fully trust it. I'd rather find the one thing that matters and strip everything else away. A lot of my work, DiT with Bill Peebles for example, was really about asking, can we just use the simplest, most scalable architecture and let scaling do the work? Simple things are also easier for other people to build on, and I think that's where the real impact comes from.

The third thing is to be honest with yourself about what you actually know. There's a lot of pressure in this field to claim more than your results support. I try to be careful about that. If the experiment says something I didn't expect, that's usually the most interesting part, not something to hide.

And maybe the last one is about people. Especially now that I'm at NYU and advising students, I think a researcher's decisions should also be about who you train and what kind of taste you pass on. Taste is this vague word, but it's real. Knowing which problems are worth your time is probably the most important skill, and you mostly learn it from working with people who have it. So I try to spend a lot of my energy there.

astra-6.text:
I think the first principle is to be honest with yourself about why you’re working on a problem. Is there something you genuinely want to understand, or are you choosing it because it’s popular and you know how to get a paper out of it? Those motivations can overlap, but it’s useful to recognize the difference.

Then, have conviction, but stay willing to change your mind. Research requires pursuing ideas before you have enough evidence to convince everyone else. At the same time, if the experiments contradict your intuition, you have to take that seriously. You shouldn’t become attached to an explanation just because it was yours.

And I would think about what you’re learning over the long term. A project might fail to produce the result you hoped for, but still help you ask a much better question. For me, that’s a useful guide: does this direction deepen my understanding and open up something worth exploring next?

r001.rationale: The response encourages changing one’s mind when experiments contradict intuition, but it does not say that a competitive research environment may erode skepticism.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts genuine curiosity with choosing popular problems, but it does not clearly advocate doing distinctive research as a guiding principle.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, curiosity is probably the most important starting point. You want to work on a question because you really want to understand the answer, not just because it’s fashionable or likely to produce a paper.

But curiosity needs to be paired with honesty. It’s very easy to become attached to an idea and then look for experiments that support it. I think you have to keep asking: What does this experiment actually tell me? What would convince me that my intuition is wrong?

I also value simplicity. If something works, can we identify the essential reason? Can we remove the extra components and still preserve the result? That process often teaches you more than adding another clever trick.

And finally, I’d try to choose questions with a longer time horizon. Research involves a lot of uncertainty, so you can’t always know whether a project will succeed. But you can ask whether answering the question would meaningfully change how we think about the problem. That’s a useful compass.
